intro:
1918 - Sailors revolt

No one still wants war, but the government does not get it. It sends the German fleet into the final battle against the Royal Navy. Your comrades defend themselves. This means mutiny. The ships turned back. The mutineers, however, were captured ...
Your comrades need help. Karl Artelt and Lothar Popp, leader of the revolt and USPD members, stand by your side. Go in and win!!

Note: The Steinhäuser Patrol is on the way to knock down the revolt ...

Historical:
The fleet had been moved from Kiel to Wilhelmshaven to set from there sail to the last battle. Despite utmost secrecy the plans came through to the crews.
Thereupon the sailors on three ships of the Third Naval Battle Squadron refused to weigh anchor for the last naval battle of WW1.
Part of the crew of SMS Thüringen and SMS Helgoland, two battle ships of the First Naval Battle Squadron, committed outright mutiny and sabotage. However, when a day later some torpedo boats directed their cannons onto these ships, the mutineers gave up and were led away without any resistance.
The fleet again entered Kiel. 47 sailors were arrested and detained at the naval base 'Wilhelm Souchon'.
Some 250 sailors met in the evening of 1 November in the Union House in Kiel and prevented the fleet from setting sail again.
The Revolution started from here with the sailor Karl Artelt and shipyard worker Lothar Popp (both USPD) as ringleaders.
The next day, police closed the Union House. Several thousand sailors and workers moved to the "Großer Exerzierplatz" (large drill ground). Under the slogan: "peace and bread" they demanded the release of the mutineers.
On 4 November the governor of the naval base, Wilhelm Souchon, gave way and let the detained sailors free. However, foreign troops marched on to defeat the movement.
These were intercepted by the rebels, captured, or joined the uprising.
On the evening of 4 November's Kiel was firmly in the hands of about 40,000 rebellious sailors, soldiers and workers.

Author = Matze (M. Kessler)

briliant.text: The revolution has begun. A wildfire can develop. Help the comrades with it ...

victory.text: The revolution has begun. A wildfire can develop. Help the comrades with it ...

tactical.text: The revolution has begun. A wildfire can develop. Help the comrades with it ...

lose.text: The revolution is over ... Many comrades have fallen. You are captured ... It is not difficult to guess that you expect death ...

dialogue.speaker: Karl Artelt
dialogue.text: Do not fold that order, comrade. Let every stoker see the Admiralty seal. Berlin is asking the Allies for an armistice, and the admirals still mean to send the High Seas Fleet against the British. They call it honour. Below decks we call it choosing our own grave.

dialogue.speaker: Karl Artelt
dialogue.text: Thüringen refused steam. Helgoland followed. The officers answered by taking forty-seven men from Markgraf; I have their names here. Two hundred and fifty sailors packed the union hall last night, and Souchon would not receive even two of us.

dialogue.speaker: Lothar Popp
dialogue.text: Then stop carrying petitions to men who answer with prison lists. The police are closing the halls. The USPD and the shipyard unions can put workers in the streets and runners on every road—but only if the fleet's refusal becomes the beginning of power, not the last protest of an isolated crew.

dialogue.speaker: Karl Artelt
dialogue.text: You ask the men to rise with us while forty-seven comrades can hear the guards working the bolts. I stood in that hall tonight, Lothar. They did not come to be told about telegraph offices. If we march past that compound to seize a switchboard, every stoker in Kiel will know exactly what our word is worth.

dialogue.speaker: Lothar Popp
dialogue.text: And if the governor keeps the station and telegraph, he seals every ship off from the yards and writes the first account of this night. The patrols already have live ammunition; before dawn they may have the depots too. The action committee put its first armed column in your hands, comrade. Do you take it to the prison or to the wires?

choices.text: The prison first. We take out whom we can through the service gate before the alarm—and we do not pretend that everyone will come out with us.
choices.hint: Gain an experienced half-strength sailor detachment from the first escape, but leave the remainder exposed in the yard and forgo the arsenals' prestige and army-wide drill.

choices.text: The station, telegraph and armouries first. Keep a rescue column ready; opening the cells means nothing if the governor seals the whole city by morning.
choices.hint: Secure the arsenals' prestige and drill every formation, but leave the prisoners behind the wall until your column reaches them; the guards will open fire as soon as you approach.

dialogue.speaker: Gustav Garbe
dialogue.text: The service gate is open—the first men are out and asking for rifles. The rest are still crossing the inner yard, and the alarm is already hammering through the base. If you want them alive, your column has to reach that compound now.

dialogue.speaker: Gustav Garbe
dialogue.text: The telegraph keys are ours, and runners are carrying your order to the armouries. The forty-seven are still behind Souchon's wall. The guards will fire as soon as they see your rescue column, so reach the compound before the crowd at the gate is scattered.

dialogue.speaker: Governor Souchon's Headquarters
dialogue.text: Order from the Governor's headquarters: all unauthorised assemblies are to disperse. Naval patrols will secure the detention compound, railway station, telegraph office and military depots. Ringleaders are to be arrested before the morning watch.

dialogue.speaker: Karl Artelt
dialogue.text: Then the morning watch will find something the admirals never planned for: sailors, soldiers and workers acting together. Disarm those who resist, accept those who join us, and keep the ships in harbour. No one is sailing out to die for an empire that has already lost its war.

orders.situation: Sailors who resisted the fleet's final battle order have been arrested. Workers are joining the protest, while the naval governor is attempting to seal meeting places and deploy loyalist patrols.
orders.mission: Turn the protest into an organised seizure of power in Kiel before outside troops can restore imperial control.
primaryObjectives: Secure the principal naval installations and armouries
Control Kiel's railway and communications centres
Defeat or disarm the loyalist suppression force
secondaryObjectives: Preserve the core sailor and worker formations
Bring isolated military detachments over to the revolution where possible
orders.enemyIntelligence: The Steinhäuser patrol and other loyalist detachments are expected to move against the uprising. Some units may surrender or change sides once the revolutionary forces demonstrate control.
orders.availableSupport: Shipyard workers, USPD organisers and sympathetic sailors are mobilising across the city.
orders.notes: Speed and control of communications matter more than destroying every loyalist formation. Avoid unnecessary fighting in civilian districts.

intro:
1918 Willhelmshafen

After Kiel, the naval base of Wilhelmshaven is now rebelling. Under the leadership of Bernhard Kuhnt, you are now the one representative for the Council of the 21, whom the revolution now badly needs
Conquer the north, Aurich, Emden and especially the reservists garrison Oldenburg!!!

Historically:

In Wilhelmshaven-Rüstringen was founded on 6th November 1918, after a mass demonstration of over 20,000 naval and shipyard workers and other civilians a workers and Soldiers Council, with its executive organ, the so-called Council or the 21.
To Chairman of the Council was appointed Bernhard Kuhnt. The "21er" Council
took over the power of the fortified towns,the North Sea Station,the encircling land of Oldenburg in Ostfriesland and all the surrounding islands, without resistance of the military station commands and declared on 10 November 1918 in front of 100,000 enthusiastic demonstrators in Wilhelmshaven,
the Socialist Republic of Oldenburg and the deposition of the Grand Duke of Oldenburg.
Under the impression of demonstrations and pressure from the large majority of Members of Parliament,Grand Duke Friedrich August of Oldenburg declared his abdication on 11 November 1918.
The Free State of Oldenburg was therefore declared in the territory of the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg.
As a provisional government was formed a Land-governing-body, to what, among others, the Rüstringer Member of Parliament Paul Hug and Kuhnt belonged.
Kuhnt became president of the new Free State of Oldenburg.
-------------------------------------

Autor = Matze (M. Kessler)

briliant.text: Well done! The revolution continues. A wildfire is developed. Keep it up!

victory.text: Well done! The revolution continues. A wildfire is developed. Keep it up!

tactical.text: Well done! The revolution continues. A wildfire is developed. Keep it up!

briefing.act: ACT II — THE COUNCILS TAKE POWER

dialogue.speaker: Marta Reimers
dialogue.text: They heard what your column did in Kiel before your train cleared the junction. Men in these yards repeat the fleet's refusal as if they stood on the decks themselves; the garrison has been arguing with itself ever since.

dialogue.speaker: Marta Reimers
dialogue.text: The casualty lists reached these yards before you did. Men still came to hear the delegate from Kiel—but the officers had time to read the same telegrams, bar the armouries and prepare for your column.

dialogue.speaker: Marta Reimers
dialogue.text: Kiel still holds behind you. That is enough to make this room listen when its delegate speaks—though the officers here have not lost their nerve, and they still command the harbour batteries.

dialogue.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
dialogue.text: Because your column held the Kiel naval base, its crews have been sending us everything they can spare. Half the rifles against this wall came north on their wagons.

dialogue.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
dialogue.text: You left Kiel with its naval base slipping back into the officers' hands. Whatever remained in those magazines will be issued to the men sent after us.

dialogue.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
dialogue.text: Your telegraph gamble paid for the journey north: our operators knew Wilhelmshaven had risen before the Admiralty did, and your train passed every signal they tried to close.

dialogue.speaker: Marta Reimers
dialogue.text: The men from the Arrestlokal came on the train behind yours. They have not let anyone forget whose column opened the gate; half the sailors in this room joined after hearing them tell it.

dialogue.speaker: Marta Reimers
dialogue.text: The sailors you pulled through the service gate came north with us, and they have not sat down since. The rest were still behind Souchon's wall when your train left. Artelt sends word that the governor may yet release them—and that he is done building plans on the governor's mercy.

dialogue.speaker: Marta Reimers
dialogue.text: I carried your despatches all that night, comrade, and I will carry this one too. The crowd went down to the Arrestlokal without us. Steinhäuser's men were across the street with the order already given - eight dead, twenty-nine carried away, and the cells still locked when the firing stopped. The telegraph worked perfectly. That is what I had to tell the families, standing in a room where the wire was the only thing that had held.

dialogue.speaker: Marta Reimers
dialogue.text: Mind the rifles against the wall; every chair in the Parkhaus is taken. Sailors in oilskins sit beside stokers, clerks and yard delegates. Hear those three telephones? Yesterday the operators carried every order from the admiral. Today they bring each one to the council first.

dialogue.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
dialogue.text: Those crumpled ballots elected the Council of 21. The admiral still has seals and letterhead in his office; he no longer has the gates, the crews or the telephone exchange. That may last an hour or a week. Your work in Kiel bought us this argument, Delegate. It did not settle it.

dialogue.speaker: Paul Hug
dialogue.text: Inside the harbour the officers hesitate. Beyond it, Aurich, Emden and Oldenburg are waiting to see whether this is a local mutiny or the beginning of a new power. The council has placed its field columns under you. Do you send them out now, or make this base impossible to retake first?

choices.text: Send columns immediately toward Aurich, Emden and Oldenburg. Political momentum will collapse if the uprising remains trapped inside the naval base.
choices.hint: Gain an untested soldiers' detachment and a prestige award, but forgo full core resupply and the entrenched infantry detachment.

choices.text: Secure the harbour, station, post and armouries first. A council without a defensible base will be dispersed by the first organised loyalist regiment.
choices.hint: Fully resupply every core formation and gain an entrenched infantry detachment, but forgo the soldiers' detachment and prestige award.

dialogue.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
dialogue.text: Agreed. Each column must carry delegates as well as rifles. We are not occupying foreign towns; we are helping their soldiers and workers form councils of their own.

dialogue.speaker: Paul Hug
dialogue.text: And if Oldenburg strikes while our rifles are scattered among three roads? I will carry the council's order, Kuhnt, but do not call speed a substitute for a defensible base. The towns may welcome our delegates; the garrison will count our battalions.

dialogue.speaker: Paul Hug
dialogue.text: Then make the base secure quickly. The Oldenburg garrison is the greatest remaining obstacle, and delay gives its officers time to isolate the coast.

dialogue.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
dialogue.text: You will have your secure harbour. Beyond it, workers who rose because Kiel moved first will watch us guard warehouses while they face their officers alone. If their courage cools before our columns arrive, fortifications will not recover it.

dialogue.speaker: Marta Reimers
dialogue.text: At every railway town, someone ties a red ribbon to my sleeve and asks whose orders your column carries. Workers will stop trains for us and soldiers will listen, but neither will risk everything until they see who controls the roads and armouries. The Oldenburg officers are counting the same rifles.

dialogue.speaker: Bernhard Kuhnt
dialogue.text: Then we make the calculation for them. Carry council resolutions with the rifles, disarm officers who organise resistance, and leave elected delegates behind every column. We are not replacing one distant command with another—we are teaching each town to command itself.

orders.situation: The Wilhelmshaven naval station has joined the revolution and elected the Council of 21. Its authority is secure inside the port but uncertain across Oldenburg and East Frisia.
orders.mission: Consolidate revolutionary control of Wilhelmshaven and carry the uprising into the surrounding towns before loyalist garrisons can organise a counterstroke.
primaryObjectives: Secure Wilhelmshaven naval base and its communications
Establish control in Aurich and Emden
Neutralise the reserve garrison at Oldenburg
Keep the routes between the coastal councils open
secondaryObjectives: Capture armouries and transport hubs intact
Encourage local soldiers to surrender or join their councils
orders.enemyIntelligence: Most naval personnel are unwilling to fight for the old command, but reserve officers and local garrisons may resist once revolutionary columns leave Wilhelmshaven.
orders.availableSupport: Sailors, shipyard workers and newly elected delegates can reinforce captured towns and maintain order.
orders.notes: The scenario dramatises the Council of 21's claimed authority over Oldenburg and East Frisia. Historically, its effective power remained concentrated mainly in Wilhelmshaven.

intro:
1918 The revolt comes upon Frankfurt

7 November

The revolution is fomented. The coastal towns are in our hands. Now freed Frankfurt on Main and conquer by this the city of Finance, or can Großherzog Ernst Ludwig of Hessen put down the rebellion?

Historical:
According to the Sailors' revolt in Kiel, the revolution spreads to Frankfurt

There they formed Workers' and Soldiers' Councils and called for the abdication of Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig of Hesse. But he refuses ...

Autor = Matze (M. Kessler)

briliant.text: Well done! The revolution continues. A wildfire is developed. Keep it up!

victory.text: Well done! The revolution continues. A wildfire is developed. Keep it up!

tactical.text: Well done! The revolution continues. A wildfire is developed. Keep it up!

lose.text: The revolution is over ... Many comrades have fallen. You are captured ... It is not difficult to guess that you expect death ...

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: News of your coastal columns arrived before your train. The stationmaster has already pushed two government troop trains onto sidings; Frankfurt's garrison has spent two days deciding whether it still takes orders.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: The casualty lists reached Frankfurt before you did. The officials have pinned them beside the government's proclamations as proof that your councils can be resisted—and the police guarding this platform believe them.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: The northern councils still hold, and their seals got your train through. But Frankfurt is not a naval town: here the old authorities still have police, officials and a printing press.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: Four telegrams, four council seals: Norden, Aurich, Emden, Oldenburg. The railwaymen carry your despatches free of charge now and leave the government's sacks on the platform.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: This handbill says your coastal rising has already been stopped. It was printed in one of the towns your columns never reached, and the police are passing copies through the barracks.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: Your speed opened every signal north of here. It also brought me formations that have not slept under a roof since Kiel. Ask them for another forced march and some will make it; do not pretend all will.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: Your column arrived fed, armed and in step. The police used those same hours to wire the telegraph room and promise hot meals in the barracks. We are about to learn which preparation mattered more.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: Keep your men off the tracks, Delegate. The locomotive crews have banked their fires. Soldiers arriving from the west tear the imperial cockades from their caps before stepping onto the platform; the police at the telegraph room pretend not to notice. Everyone is waiting for someone else to move first.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: The railwaymen will stop troop trains for your column, but they will not hand you Frankfurt. Lose these stations and every council delegate in the city becomes a name on a police list. Hold them, and no loyalist company moves without our permission.

dialogue.speaker: Otto Weber
dialogue.text: The barracks are split. One company has elected delegates, another has locked its armoury, and the officers are promising food and order to anyone who obeys. Until Frankfurt elects its council, the soldiers' delegates will follow your field orders. What does the city see first: the council speaking in public, or the old state losing control of its machinery?

choices.text: Occupy the Hauptbahnhof, bridges, post and telegraph. Once communications are ours, the authorities cannot coordinate a suppression force.
choices.hint: Gain a prestige award and experience for every core formation, but forgo the two additional worker battalions.

choices.text: Call a mass assembly and proclaim the council before moving on the barracks. Political legitimacy will bring hesitant soldiers over to us.
choices.hint: Raise two worker battalions and earn their later political support, but pay prestige and forgo core-wide experience.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Jakob Adler
dialogue.text: Take the switchboards, then—but do not confuse machinery with consent. If the square sees armed soldiers before it sees an elected council, the old officials will call this another occupation and some workers will believe them. A revolution that cannot deliver bread will lose the streets it wins.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: The railwaymen will open the stations to the council, not to a new barracks command. But Adler is right about one thing: seize a telegraph office without explaining whose orders it carries, and fear will explain it for us.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: The unions can fill the square before noon, and soldiers who will not follow a secret committee may follow a council elected in front of them. But while the speeches are being made, trusted crews must close the stations to hostile troop movements.

dialogue.speaker: Otto Weber
dialogue.text: A public mandate may bring hesitant companies over. It will not stop the troop train already signalled from the west. Give the speeches their square, but if the railway crews wait for the vote before pulling that signal, legitimacy will arrive under guard.

dialogue.speaker: Loyalist District Command
dialogue.text: All railway, postal and municipal facilities are to remain under lawful authority. Armed councils will be dispersed and military property recovered.

dialogue.speaker: Otto Weber
dialogue.text: Then every company receives the same offer: elect delegates and keep its weapons under council authority, or be disarmed. Frankfurt must choose before Berlin chooses for it—and the railway must carry that choice east.

orders.situation: The revolution has spread inland. Frankfurt has formed a workers' and soldiers' council, but the municipal administration and military authorities still possess functioning institutions and armed detachments.
orders.mission: Secure the city's communications and strategic centres, expand support for the council and prevent the uprising from being divided and suppressed.
primaryObjectives: Capture Frankfurt's principal railway and communications centres
Secure the bridges and designated government objectives
Disarm or defeat organised loyalist detachments
Maintain a continuous revolutionary zone through the city
secondaryObjectives: Preserve worker and soldier formations for the march on Berlin
Avoid unnecessary damage to transport infrastructure
orders.enemyIntelligence: The loyalists have fewer supporters than the council but retain officers, police, barracks and the ability to move troops by rail if the main stations remain open.
orders.availableSupport: Railway workers can obstruct hostile movement, while sympathetic soldiers may join after the council demonstrates control of the city.
orders.notes: The original scenario combines events in Frankfurt with the fall of the neighbouring Grand Duchy of Hesse. Frankfurt itself had been part of Prussia since 1866, and its historical workers' and soldiers' council exercised only limited influence over the city government.

intro:
1918 End of the Monarchy

When the Emperor heard of the revolts in Kiel, he orderd the 4th Jäger Regiment to Berlin. The city burns. The insurgents have the working-class neighborhoods under control.

Can Police and Jäger put down the rebellion? Or has the Kaiser to quit and leave Berlin?

there is little support announced for both sides ..

Historical :
In reality, everything went bloodless. After the revolt in Kiel, Wilhelmshaven and other towns the USPD planned in Berlin mass demonstrations and a general strike for the 9th November 1918 . This was heard by the competing SPD under leadership of its chairman, Friedrich Ebert.

In order to remain master of the situation,

To anticipate the USPD, Ebert forced Chancellor Max von Baden to announce the abdication of Wilhelm II.
The Kaiser was this time at Spa, where the allied armistice terms had been previously negotiated. He then fled to his Dutch exile where he signed the abdication on 28.11.1919.

Autor = Matze (M. Kessler)

briliant.text: Well done! The revolution is successful! Long live the Republic!

victory.text: Well done! The revolution is successful! Long live the Republic!

tactical.text: Well done! The revolution is successful! Long live the Republic!

lose.text: The revolution is over ... Many comrades have fallen. You are captured ... It is not difficult to guess that you expect death ...

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: The delegates at Lehrter station were arguing over whether your column could possibly arrive intact. Then it marched off the train before they finished. Berlin is the last question, comrade, and for once we ask it from strength.

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: Your column reached Berlin behind its own casualty lists. The Majority Socialists are reading those names when they speak of order and continuity, and frightened people will listen to them.

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: They know your column in the working districts now. What they do not know is whether Berlin will turn the councils' movement into power—or into a negotiation conducted over their heads.

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: Word that you armed the workers in Frankfurt reached Berlin yesterday. Our factory battalions are in the streets now; they did not wait to be asked. That is our strength—and exactly what the Majority Socialists point to when they call for order.

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: Every city you crossed was meant to be isolated before the next one moved. Instead your trains carried delegates, rifles and confidence toward Berlin. The ministries assumed obedience would travel faster than revolt; this week proved the opposite.

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: You left Frankfurt with its city, bridges and station under council guard. The Rhine-Main delegates arriving behind you carry mandates now, not petitions.

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: You had to leave Frankfurt before its council closed its hand on the whole city. The government still has a functioning administration in the west, and it is using it against us.

dialogue.speaker: Anna Keller
dialogue.text: You told us to take the railway before the proclamations. We did. The government still has telephones, but the delegates arriving at Berlin carry our orders and our account of Frankfurt. Do not waste what we bought you.

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: Listen—the factory whistles began before dawn and have not stopped. Columns are leaving Moabit, Wedding and the eastern works; soldiers at the gates argue over whether the Kaiser has already abdicated. Inside the ministries, clerks keep stamping imperial forms as if paper could hold the city together.

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: Those columns are the general strike made visible: workers leaving machines, soldiers electing councils, prison gates and barracks opening before the crowds. The old government still occupies the centre, but obedience is draining out of it by the hour. If we wait for the ministries to admit that, Ebert will be inside them first.

dialogue.speaker: Hugo Haase
dialogue.text: Karl, a republic proclaimed from the street can still starve in the street. Millions who want the Kaiser gone do not all want the councils to replace elections. If we make every clerk and returning soldier choose between Ebert and civil war today, fear will choose for them.

dialogue.speaker: Karl Liebknecht
dialogue.text: And a ministry can call elections while the old officers, judges and police remain at their desks. Ebert offers continuity because he fears chaos; I fear continuity because it can bury the revolution without restoring the Kaiser. Delegate, which danger does your column answer first?

choices.text: Drive directly toward the Reichstag and government quarter. The revolution must visibly replace imperial authority.
choices.hint: Gain a prestige award and experience for every core formation, but forgo full resupply and the experienced sailor detachment.

choices.text: Secure the barracks, stations and telegraph offices first. No proclamation will survive if loyalist troops control Berlin's communications.
choices.hint: Fully resupply every core formation and gain an experienced sailor detachment, but forgo the government-quarter prestige and core-wide experience.

dialogue.speaker: Hugo Haase
dialogue.text: Then you have chosen Liebknecht's symbol over my caution. I will not obstruct the march, but symbols do not feed columns or keep soldiers together. Maintain contact with the workers' districts and barracks—or the government quarter will become a stage surrounded by someone else's troops.

dialogue.speaker: Emil Barth
dialogue.text: Then the stations and telegraph offices must fall in the first hours. Stop military trains, seize government messages, and make every captured barracks elect delegates. We need obedience to pass from the officers to the councils, not merely buildings to change hands.

dialogue.speaker: Karl Liebknecht
dialogue.text: Necessary—and politically timid. Every hour spent securing a signal box is an hour in which the Majority Socialists speak for the revolution from imperial offices. Win your barracks, Delegate. Then decide whether you have preserved the councils' power or merely made Ebert's republic safe.

dialogue.speaker: SPD Headquarters
dialogue.text: Political dispatch from SPD headquarters: Friedrich Ebert calls for order, food distribution, an armistice government and elections. He warns that civil war will destroy the republic before it is born. The ministries are preparing to survive the fall of the Kaiser.

dialogue.speaker: Karl Liebknecht
dialogue.text: Then enter the centre as an organised force, not a crowd waiting for permission. Break the last armed resistance, open the prisons and government quarter, and make certain that when the monarchy falls, power does not simply pass from a uniform to a ministerial desk.

orders.situation: A general strike and mass demonstrations are paralysing Berlin. Revolutionary columns control many working-class districts, while police, guards and Jäger detachments defend key institutions and transport routes.
orders.mission: Unite the revolutionary districts, seize the capital's centres of government and communication, and prevent loyalist forces from restoring imperial authority.
primaryObjectives: Capture Berlin's government quarter and designated political objectives
Secure the main railway stations and telegraph facilities
Defeat or disarm the police and Jäger suppression forces
secondaryObjectives: Maintain contact between the advancing revolutionary columns
Preserve enough organised forces to hold the capital after victory
Prevent isolated loyalist units from reopening routes into the centre
orders.enemyIntelligence: Loyalist units are politically uncertain but remain dangerous around government buildings, barracks and transport hubs. Some may refuse to fire if confronted by massed workers and soldiers.
orders.availableSupport: The general strike restricts government movement. Workers' delegates and sympathetic soldiers can consolidate captured districts and bring additional formations into the councils.
orders.notes: The scenario presents a more militarised struggle than most events in Berlin on 9 November, which were largely peaceful despite several fatal shootings. Max von Baden announced the Kaiser's abdication, Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a republic, and Karl Liebknecht proclaimed a socialist republic later that day.

epilogues.speaker: Emil Barth
epilogues.text: Berlin saw organised council columns enter the political centre before imperial authority could disguise its retreat. The monarchy has fallen, but Haase was right about the next struggle: tomorrow the councils must decide whether they govern beside the new republic or surrender power to it.

epilogues.speaker: Hugo Haase
epilogues.text: You made the government quarter the measure of the revolution and concentrated every enemy around it. The surviving councils will remember the courage of the march—and argue for years over whether its symbol cost them the organised force they needed.

epilogues.speaker: Karl Liebknecht
epilogues.text: Your stations and barracks made the revolution harder to crush, Delegate. They also gave Ebert time to inherit the ministries while the councils secured his communications. The monarchy has fallen; whether power changed hands or merely changed its uniform remains unsettled.

epilogues.speaker: Emil Barth
epilogues.text: We held messages, platforms and armouries, but never joined them into power. The old command recovered one institution at a time. Survivors will say your caution preserved them; others will say it taught the revolution to defend buildings instead of deciding who governed.
